addressed_problems.content: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) offer event-driven, sparse computation and low power consumption desirable for edge devices, but state-of-the-art spiking Transformer architectures (notably Spikformer) combine Transformer self-attention with SNN elements at the cost of substantially enlarged MLP channel dimensions and many redundant weight parameters. Prior practice computes attention and MLP updates over all image patch tokens and retains large MLP hidden dimensions, which (a) increases floating-point computation (FLOPs) and inference latency, (b) inflates model parameter storage and memory accesses, and (c) prevents efficient deployment on resource-constrained hardware despite the inherent spike sparsity of SNNs. Existing SNN and Transformer optimizations had not been demonstrated as a co-designed token-and-weight pruning approach tailored to Spikformer: there was no established, differentiable token-importance mechanism that leverages spiking activity to drop uninformative image tokens before attention, nor an evaluated application of Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) style iterative magnitude pruning specifically targeted at Spikformer MLP/attention weights with practical pruning schedules. As a result, practitioners lacked a validated method to (i) remove background or low-activity tokens from the spiking attention pipeline in a differentiable way while controlling per-layer keep ratios, and (ii) obtain highly sparse Spikformer subnetworks (large weight compression, e.g., >~90% pruning) that retain competitive accuracy—preventing quantitative claims about combined token+weight sparsification trade-offs (accuracy vs. GFLOPs vs. parameter count) and hindering deployment on edge accelerators.

nodes.content: In Spikformer, attention and MLP computations are executed over all patch tokens regardless of their spiking activity; this wastes compute on background or low-activity regions. Prior token-reduction strategies for vision Transformers (e.g., heuristic token dropping) do not exploit the temporal spike activity available in SNNs and are not formulated as a lightweight, differentiable module compatible with spiking attention. Consequently, there was no published mechanism that (a) computes a compact per-token importance score from spike trains, (b) yields differentiable binary keep/drop decisions suitable for end-to-end training inside a spiking Encoder block, and (c) composes decisions across encoder layers. Without such a module, researchers could not systematically reduce attention input cardinality in Spikformer while preserving the ability to train selection jointly with the network.

A single global token keep percentage is insufficient because encoder layers have different roles and attention costs; to realize practical runtime and FLOPs reductions one must specify where in the encoder to drop tokens and how aggressively to reduce token counts per layer. Prior works on Transformer token pruning did not provide an experimentally validated insertion schedule tailored to Spikformer’s spiking computation pipeline. Without an explicit layer-wise pruning schedule and insertion points, it is unclear how to trade off early-layer representational richness against downstream compute savings and how to realize cumulative reductions in attention complexity in the spiking setting.

Spikformer’s MLP-heavy architecture produces many parameters concentrated in fully connected layers, and although SNN activations are temporally sparse, that activation sparsity does not by itself guarantee weight-level redundancy; a method was needed to determine whether extreme parameter pruning (to >~90% sparsity) could produce trainable subnetworks (winning tickets) inside Spikformer. Prior LTH demonstrations focused primarily on ANNs and some SNN settings but had not been established for Spikformer’s combined spiking-attention/MLP architecture with a concrete iterative pruning schedule and rewinding policy. Without such an application and empirical validation, claims about safe weight compression for Spikformer remained unsubstantiated.

Transformers incur quadratic (or at least high) attention-related FLOPs in the number of tokens and MLP computations scale with channel width; in Spikformer this cost is magnified by the default practice of keeping all tokens through all encoder layers. To deploy spiking Transformers on constrained hardware, practitioners need concrete, measured trade-offs showing that selective token removal (guided by spike activity) can materially reduce FLOPs and wall-clock inference throughput without losing accuracy. Prior work lacked Spikformer-specific throughput and FLOPs numbers showing that a time-averaged spiking activity criterion can safely remove a substantial fraction of tokens and yield measurable runtime and FLOPs reductions.

Weight storage and memory access dominate energy and latency on many platforms; if Spikformer’s large MLP parameterization could be reduced by an order of magnitude without harming accuracy, it would directly address storage bottlenecks. Before this work, it was unclear whether LTH-style IMP would identify trainable winning tickets inside a spiking Transformer architecture up to extreme sparsity levels (near 90% weight removal) and whether token pruning plus weight pruning together would preserve accuracy. Quantitative per-dataset accuracy numbers at multiple sparsity levels were required to assess whether weight pruning alone or in combination with token pruning is a viable route to compress Spikformer for edge use.

Multiple LTH variants and re-initialization strategies exist, but their relative effectiveness for spiking Transformer architectures was unsettled. Practitioners needed to know whether lightweight early-exit or early-bird style identification (EB) or simpler RR strategies could match the performance of full iterative magnitude pruning, and whether rewinding to earlier iterates is necessary. Without head-to-head comparisons and quantitative margins, it was unclear which pruning/reinitialization recipe should be adopted for Spikformer compression.

Single-axis optimizations (only token reduction or only weight pruning) address compute or storage in isolation; however, practical edge deployment requires both reduced parameter storage and lower attention/MLP FLOPs. Prior to this co-design, there was no empirical demonstration that (a) a spiking-activity-driven token selector can combine with LTH-style weight pruning to simultaneously deliver dramatic parameter compression (>~90% reduction) and meaningful FLOPs/throughput improvements, and (b) that doing so preserves accuracy across both static and neuromorphic datasets. Without a combined empirical result, claims about end-to-end hardware friendliness of spiking Transformers remained speculative.

A lightweight, differentiable Spiking Token Selector (STS) is formulated to evaluate and decide which image patch tokens participate in subsequent Spiking Self-Attention (SSA) and MLP computations. Given an input spiking tensor $X\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times N\times D}$ (temporal length $T$, $N$ tokens, token feature dimension $D$), STS computes
      $$
      X' = \text{GAP}(X),\quad X'\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D},
      $$
      where $\text{GAP}(\cdot)$ denotes global average pooling along the temporal axis. The pooled per-token features $X'$ are fed to a two-layer MLP followed by Softmax to produce keep/drop logits
      $$
      S = \text{Softmax}(\text{MLP}(X')),\quad S\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times 2},
      $$
      where the two columns of $S$ are interpreted as the per-token probabilities for the classes {keep, drop}. A differentiable binary decision vector is obtained by applying the Gumbel-Softmax reparameterization to the keep-column:
      $$
      \mathbf{D} = \text{Gumbel-Softmax}(S_{\ast,1}),\quad \mathbf{D}\in\{0,1\}^N.
      $$
      Across encoder layers the current layer decision is combined with previous decisions via element-wise multiplication
      $$
      \hat{\mathbf{D}} = \hat{\mathbf{D}}\odot\mathbf{D},
      $$
      yielding the final per-token keep mask used to select the top-$\rho\%$ (where $\rho$ is the keep ratio, the fraction of tokens retained) tokens for attention/MLP. This STS explicitly uses spiking activity averaged over time as the input criterion and produces differentiable, trainable token selection decisions suitable for insertion into a Spikformer encoder.

metadata.narrative: No load-bearing weak points were identified in the derivation of the STS formulation itself, as the module is explicitly defined by its mathematical operations and architectural insertion. The paper's derivation of the formulation is a direct construction without reliance on uncertain empirical or modeling steps. Effectiveness of the STS is contingent on factors evaluated in Conclusions 4 and 7, which carry separate premises.

nodes.title: Spiking Token Selector (STS) — differentiable token-importance scoring and binary keep decisions

nodes.content: Token pruning is applied dynamically at multiple encoder depths with a layer-wise keep-rate schedule: the Spiking Token Selector (STS) is inserted after the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th encoder layers, and the pruning schedule progressively reduces token count across layers using multiplicative keep-rate factors such that the keep ratios are $[\rho, \rho^2, \rho^3]$, where $\rho$ is the keep ratio (the fraction of tokens retained), so that each downstream block receives fewer tokens. At each insertion point, the top $\rho\%$ tokens, as determined by the STS decisions, are selected to feed into the Spiking Self-Attention (SSA) and Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) modules, controlling per-layer computational cost while allowing earlier layers to operate on denser token sets.

metadata.narrative: The layer-wise token pruning schedule is explicitly described by its insertion points and multiplicative keep-rate factors; the derivation is a design specification without uncertain empirical claims. Thus, no weak points or highlights were found; the schedule is a stated design choice that does not rely on unproven bridges.

nodes.title: Layer-wise token pruning schedule with multiplicative keep-rate factors after the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th encoder layers

nodes.content: Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) following the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) paradigm is applied to Spikformer (and to the token-pruned SparseSpikformer) to obtain binary connectivity masks $M\in\{0,1\}$ such that the subnetwork $f(x;M\odot\theta)$ retains competitive accuracy. The IMP workflow used is: randomly initialize a dense network $f(x;\theta)$, train to convergence, rank weights by absolute magnitude, prune the smallest $p\%$ weights, reinitialize the remaining weights (rewinding), and repeat for $K$ iterations. In experiments the hyperparameters were set to $p=25$ and $K=15$, producing extreme pruning levels (iterated removals) that yield subnetworks with only about 10% of original parameters preserved (i.e., >~90% sparsity). This approach identifies sparse winning tickets in both Spikformer and SparseSpikformer that can be retrained to recover original-level accuracy.

metadata.narrative: The existence of winning tickets in Spikformer via IMP rests primarily on the empirical accuracy numbers in Table 2. Premise P1 identifies that these numbers come from single runs, making the reproducibility of the reported parity uncertain (layer: error/uncertainty quantification). Highlight H1 partially offsets this by showing consistent retention across four datasets, providing generalization support (layer: generalization). The dominant risk is statistical unreliability (P1), which is not fully offset because H1 does not address within-dataset variability. Thus, the conclusion is probable but not robust to seed variation.

nodes.title: Application of Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) under the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) to Spikformer and SparseSpikformer

nodes.content: Empirical evaluation of the Spiking Token Selector (STS)-enabled token pruning across multiple keep ratios demonstrates concrete compute and runtime gains while maintaining Top-1 accuracy. Example numbers on CIFAR-10: baseline Spikformer (keep ratio 1.0) achieves Top-1 accuracy 94.95%, throughput 950.28 samples/s, and FLOPs 3.74G; with token pruning at keep ratio $\rho=0.7$, SparseSpikformer attains Top-1 accuracy 95.01%, throughput 1448.71 samples/s, and FLOPs 3.04G. Across the evaluated datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, DVS-128) and keep ratios, token pruning reduces FLOPs by approximately 22.49% to 26.47% and increases throughput by 21.98% to 66.96% with only minimal accuracy degradation or even small accuracy gains in some cases.

metadata.narrative: The quantified compute benefits (throughput/FLOPs) of token pruning are subject to Premise P2's uncertainty about measurement generalizability; the accuracy preservation is subject to Premise P3's single-seed limitation. Highlight H2 provides a dense empirical mapping across five keep ratios and four datasets, strengthening the trade-off curve's internal consistency. Highlight H3 validates the STS criterion against random, supporting the attribution of gains to the spiking activity criterion. However, neither highlight addresses the external validity of throughput/FLOPs numbers or the within-dataset statistical robustness of accuracy. Thus, the core trade-off is qualitatively supported but quantitatively imprecise.

nodes.title: Quantified token-pruning benefits: FLOPs, throughput, and accuracy trade-offs

nodes.content: Applying Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) based on the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH) to both Spikformer and SparseSpikformer finds highly sparse subnetworks that preserve accuracy. Sparsity denotes the percentage of weights pruned from the overall model parameters. Representative results on CIFAR-10: Spikformer at 93.90% sparsity yields Top-1 accuracy 94.34%, while SparseSpikformer (with token keep ratio $\rho=0.7$, where $\rho$ is the fraction of tokens retained) at 93.90% sparsity yields Top-1 accuracy 94.97%. The experiments report multiple sparsity levels (e.g., 75.90%, 86.22%, 93.90%) with only minor accuracy drop across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS and DVS-128, demonstrating that weight pruning can reduce model parameter count by approximately 90% while retaining competitive performance.

metadata.narrative: The weight pruning results are subject to Premise P4 (single-seed accuracy, layer: error/uncertainty). Highlight H4 provides multi-dataset generalization support similar to H1 for C3. The conclusion that ∼90% parameter reduction preserves accuracy is empirically demonstrated for the reported runs, but statistical robustness is not established.

nodes.title: Quantified weight-pruning results: winning tickets at high sparsity

nodes.content: In comparisons among pruning and re-initialization strategies on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) consistently outperforms Early-Bird (EB) and Random Re-initialization (RR) when evaluating high-sparsity subnetworks. Quantitatively, IMP achieves superior Top-1 accuracy by margins of approximately 3.52% to 9.74% over EB and RR across the sparsity levels examined (75.90%, 86.22%, and 93.90% for CIFAR-10; 75.90%, 86.23%, and 92.04% for CIFAR-100). Additionally, the weight rewinding strategy used with IMP (reinitializing the remaining unpruned weights to their initial random values) produces winning-ticket accuracies closer to the dense network than simple random re-initialization (RR).

metadata.narrative: The claim that IMP outperforms EB and RR is supported by substantial margins (Highlight H5) that are consistent across static datasets. However, Premise P5 raises a comparative fairness concern: EB's hyperparameters and adaptation are not specified, so the margin may partly reflect suboptimal EB tuning. Premise P6 notes that the comparison is limited to static datasets, limiting generalization to neuromorphic inputs. Thus, the comparative ranking is valid for the evaluated setting but may not extend to all pruning contexts.

nodes.title: IMP outperforms Early-Bird (EB) and Random Re-initialization (RR); weight rewinding outperforms RR

nodes.content: The co-design of Spiking Token Selector (STS) token pruning and Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH)-based weight pruning, called SparseSpikformer, yields simultaneous storage and compute savings: the framework can produce subnetworks that retain approximately 10% of original weights (i.e., >~90% parameter pruning) and realize Giga Floating-Point Operations (GFLOPs) reductions on the order of ~20% (token pruning alone reduces FLOPs by 22.49% to 26.47%), while maintaining Top-1 accuracy comparable to the original Spikformer across CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and DVS-128. The combined approach also improves inference throughput substantially (e.g., on CIFAR-10, throughput increased from 950.28 samples/s to 1448.71 samples/s at $\rho=0.7$ token keep ratio), indicating that joint token-and-weight pruning is an effective route to reduce computational and storage requirements while preserving accuracy.

metadata.narrative: The overall co-design claim aggregates evidence from token and weight pruning. Premises P7 and P8 carry over statistical and measurement uncertainties from the constituent evaluations. Premise P9 adds that the contribution of each technique is not isolated, so the added value of the co-design over single-axis pruning is not established. Highlight H6 shows that the combined method works on four datasets, providing empirical evidence for the feasibility of simultaneous pruning. The interaction between the two pruning techniques remains undetermined; the conclusion that the co-design is synergistic is not supported, but the practical result that a heavily compressed model works is credible within the measured regime.

nodes.title: Overall co-design outcome: combined token-and-weight pruning yields ~90% parameter reduction and ~20% GFLOPs reduction while preserving accuracy

metadata.weakness_reason: In deep learning experiments, a single training run can produce results that differ by 0.5–1% or more depending on random seed, weight initialization, and data shuffle order. Without multiple seeds showing consistent outcomes, it is uncertain whether the observed accuracy at high sparsity (e.g., 94.34% on CIFAR-10 at 93.90% sparsity) is reproducible and not a statistical outlier.

metadata.failure_mode: If the throughput and FLOPs measurements are not reproducible or hardware-specific, the quantified savings (e.g., throughput increase of 21.98–66.96% and FLOPs reduction of 22.49–26.47%) cannot be claimed as general properties of SparseSpikformer; the conclusion that token pruning yields these benefits would be restricted to the unreported experimental setup, reducing its practical value.
metadata.weakness_reason: Throughput measurements are highly sensitive to hardware, batch size, data loading overhead, and implementation details (e.g., fused operations, memory bandwidth). The paper provides no description of these factors; the FLOPs appear to be theoretical reductions based on token count without accounting for the overhead of the STS module or sparsity-aware kernels. Thus, the reported throughput and FLOPs numbers may not replicate on other platforms or even on the same GPU with different configurations.

nodes.title: No interaction ablation

nodes.content: IMP weight pruning is applied to four datasets spanning static (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100) and neuromorphic (CIFAR10-DVS, DVS-128) types; at the highest sparsity level on each dataset, the Top-1 accuracy remains within 0.61–2.4% of the original Spikformer baseline (Table 2), demonstrating that winning tickets exist across diverse input modalities.

metadata.credit: This multi-dataset evaluation preempts the failure mode that winning tickets exist only on a specific dataset type. By showing consistent accuracy retention on event-based data (DVS-128 retains 98.26% at 95.8% sparsity), the conclusion that LTH produces sparse subnetworks in Spikformer gains support for generalization to neuromorphic tasks. The scope of credit is regime-bounded to these datasets, but the diversity strengthens the claim beyond a single-domain demonstration.

nodes.title: Multi-dataset weight pruning validation

nodes.content: Table 1 reports token pruning results across five keep ratios (1.0, 0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6, 0.5) on four datasets, with FLOPs reduction ranging from 22.49% to 26.47% and throughput increase from 21.98% to 66.96% across all datasets, while Top-1 accuracy changes by at most -0.18% to +0.27% relative to baseline (keep ratio 1.0) on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100.

metadata.credit: This systematic sweep preempts the failure mode that the token pruning benefit arises from a single favorable operating point. By showing monotonic compute savings and stable accuracy across a range of keep ratios on multiple datasets, the conclusion that STS provides consistent compute-accuracy trade-offs is quantitatively supported. The layer underwritten is the quantitative magnitude and direction of the trade-off. The scope of credit is full underwriting for the evaluated range on these datasets.

nodes.title: Systematic keep-ratio sweep

nodes.content: On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, and DVS-128, the Spiking Token Selector achieves higher Top-1 accuracy than a random token selector across keep ratios 0.8, 0.7, and 0.6 (Table 3), with margins up to 4.7% on CIFAR-100 at keep ratio 0.6.

metadata.credit: This comparison directly preempts the failure mode that the spike-firing-rate criterion is no better than random selection, which would undermine the claim that the STS is an effective pruning mechanism. The consistent accuracy advantage shows that the criterion captures meaningful token relevance. The layer underwritten is mechanism/attribution: the improvement is attributable to the spiking activity criterion. The scope of credit is regime-bounded to the tested datasets and keep ratios.

nodes.title: STS vs random selector comparison

nodes.content: Table 2 reports weight pruning results on four datasets; at the highest sparsity for each dataset (e.g., 93.90% on CIFAR-10, 92.04% on CIFAR-100, 95.8% on CIFAR10-DVS and DVS-128), the Top-1 accuracy stays within 0.61% to 2.16% of the Spikformer baseline (Table 1).

metadata.credit: Similar to H1, this multi-dataset evaluation preempts the failure mode that extreme weight sparsity degrades accuracy only on certain datasets. The consistent retention across static and neuromorphic data supports the conclusion that weight pruning can reduce parameters by ~90% while maintaining competitive performance. The scope of credit is full demonstration for these datasets.

metadata.credit: The large margins guard against the failure mode that IMP's advantage is marginal or varies with sparsity. The consistency across three sparsity levels and two datasets supports the conclusion that IMP is the recommended pruning method for Spikformer. The layer underwritten is comparative ranking: the relative ordering is clear. The scope of credit is regime-bounded (static datasets only), but the margins are practically meaningful.

nodes.title: IMP margins over EB and RR

nodes.content: SparseSpikformer with token keep ratio 0.7 and weight pruning up to 93.90% sparsity is evaluated on CIFAR-10 (Top-1 94.97% vs. baseline 94.95%), CIFAR-100 (75.12% vs. 77.28%), CIFAR10-DVS (76.2% vs. 78.3%), and DVS-128 (98.26% vs. 98.26%), showing that the combined pruning preserves accuracy within 0.02–2.1% while reducing parameters by ~90% and FLOPs by ~19%.

metadata.credit: This direct evaluation preempts the failure mode that simultaneous token and weight pruning would cause unacceptable accuracy loss. The fact that across four datasets the accuracy remains close to baseline (and on DVS-128 equal) demonstrates that the co-design does not compound degradation. The layer underwritten is qualitative direction and quantitative magnitude: the combined method works. The scope of credit is full demonstrated performance for the tested configuration.

nodes.title: Successful combined evaluation

steps.reasoning: Define the input spiking tensor $X\\in\\mathbb{R}^{T\\times N\\times D}$ where $T$ is the temporal length (number of time steps), $N$ is the number of image patch tokens, and $D$ is the token feature dimension; state that the STS operates on this tensor as the paper establishes the problem setting.

Apply temporal global average pooling (GAP) to $X$ to collapse the temporal axis: compute $X' = \\text{GAP}(X)$ so that $X'\\in\\mathbb{R}^{N\\times D}$; here $\\text{GAP}(\\cdot)$ denotes averaging over the temporal dimension $T$, producing one $D$-dimensional feature vector per token (this is presented as the first processing equation for the STS).

Pass the pooled per-token features $X'\\in\\mathbb{R}^{N\\times D}$ through a two-layer multilayer perceptron (MLP) consisting of two linear layers (the paper specifies "consisting of only two linear layers") and then apply a Softmax operation across the two output dimensions to obtain per-token keep/drop logits: $S = \\text{Softmax}(\\text{MLP}(X'))$ with $S\\in\\mathbb{R}^{N\\times 2}$; define that the two columns of $S$ correspond to the per-token class probabilities for {keep, drop}.

Obtain a differentiable binary decision vector by applying the Gumbel-Softmax reparameterization to the keep-class column: define $S_{*,1}$ as the first column (keep logits) of $S$, and compute $\\mathbf{D} = \\text{Gumbel-Softmax}(S_{*,1})$ with $\\mathbf{D}\\in\\{0,1\\}^N$; note that the use of Gumbel-Softmax makes the discrete keep/drop decisions amenable to gradient-based training while yielding binary decisions at inference; cite the categorical reparameterization method used.
[19]

When STS is applied across multiple encoder layers, combine the current layer's decision with previous layers' decisions by element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication: denote the accumulated decision vector as $\\hat{\\mathbf{D}}$ and update it via $\\hat{\\mathbf{D}} = \\hat{\\mathbf{D}} \\odot \\mathbf{D}$ so that once a token is dropped at any earlier layer it remains dropped for later layers according to the paper's sequential decision rule; define $\\odot$ as element-wise product.

Interpret the final per-token keep mask $\\hat{\\mathbf{D}}$ to select the top-$\\rho\\%$ tokens for subsequent Spiking Self-Attention (SSA) and MLP computations: define the keep rate $\\rho$ as the fraction of tokens preserved and state that the STS's outputs are used to feed only the retained tokens into downstream SSA and MLP modules, as described in the architecture diagram and text.
Fig. 1

State the motivating criterion for token importance used by the STS: the STS explicitly uses spiking activity averaged over time (the GAP-pooled firing-rate features $X'$) as the per-token importance signal, thereby grounding token scoring in spiking neuron activity rather than raw RGB activations.
Fig. 2

Summarize the STS as a lightweight, differentiable module suitable for insertion into the Spikformer encoder: it (a) compresses temporal spike information via GAP to per-token features $X'$, (b) computes keep/drop probabilities with a two-layer MLP and Softmax yielding $S\\in\\mathbb{R}^{N\\times 2}$, (c) converts probabilities into binary decisions $\\mathbf{D}\\in\\{0,1\\}^N$ with Gumbel-Softmax, and (d) composes decisions across layers via $\\hat{\\mathbf{D}}=\\hat{\\mathbf{D}}\\odot\\mathbf{D}$ to produce the mask used to select top-$\\rho\\%$ tokens for SSA and MLP.

Define the per-layer keep-rate $\\rho$ as the fraction (between 0 and 1) of tokens to retain at a pruning insertion point; state that the token selector outputs per-token decisions that are converted into a mask used to select the top-$\\rho\\%$ tokens for downstream computation.

Specify the practical insertion points: the token selector is inserted after the 2nd, 3rd, and 4th encoder layers of the Spikformer encoder during training and inference, as stated in the experimental setup; define "encoder layer" as one encoder block layer in the Spikformer architecture.
Fig. 1

Describe the layer-wise keep-rate scheduling used in practice: employ multiplicative keep-rate factors so that successive pruning reduces the number of tokens progressively, for example preserving token fractions $[\\rho,\\rho^2,\\rho^3]$ across the three insertion points (this schedule is the paper's example of progressively fewer tokens fed to downstream blocks).

Explain the operational effect of the schedule: earlier encoder layers operate on denser token sets (higher token counts) which allows richer low-level processing, while each downstream block receives fewer tokens according to the multiplicative schedule, thus controlling per-layer computational cost by reducing the number of tokens input to SSA and MLP at later layers.

Note that during experiments the authors implement dynamic pruning across encoder depths by "gradually removing a fraction of tokens before each block" and explicitly give the example $[\\rho,\\rho^2,\\rho^3]$ and provide a visualization of this token-pruning process for illustration (the visual confirms that a sequence of token counts is applied across encoder layers).
Fig. 3

State the objective of weight pruning under the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis (LTH): find a binary mask $M\\in\\{0,1\\}$ such that the masked subnetwork $f(x;M\\odot\\theta)$, where $f(x;\\theta)$ is the original dense network parameterized by $\\theta$, can be trained to competitive accuracy; cite the original LTH work when the paper references the hypothesis.
[18]

Describe the Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) workflow used to implement LTH in the experiments: (a) randomly initialize a dense network $f(x;\\theta)$, (b) train it to convergence, (c) rank weights by absolute magnitude $|\\theta_i|$, (d) prune the smallest $p\\%$ of weights (set corresponding mask entries in $M$ to 0), (e) reinitialize or rewind the remaining weights (apply the mask to the reinitialized weights to form $f(x;M\\odot\\theta)$), and (f) repeat the process for $K$ iterations; cite the IMP stabilization reference as used by the authors.
[21]

Record the hyperparameter choices used in the paper's experiments: set the pruning fraction per iteration $p=25$ (i.e., remove 25% of remaining weights on each IMP iteration) and set the number of IMP iterations $K=15$; define that after $K$ iterations, the fraction of weights preserved is approximately $(1-p/100)^K$ and the fraction pruned approaches very high sparsity.

Compute the practical sparsity regime achieved with $p=25$ and $K=15$ as reported: report that these settings produce "extreme pruning levels" leaving subnetworks with roughly $\\sim10\\%$ of original parameters preserved (the paper reports that experiments yield subnetworks with only about 10% of original parameters preserved, i.e., greater than approximately 90% sparsity).

State that IMP is applied to both the original Spikformer and the token-pruned SparseSpikformer variants in experiments; indicate that the resulting binary masks $M$ identify "winning tickets" (sparse subnetworks) in both model families that can be retrained to recover accuracy comparable to the dense networks, as reported in the experimental results and tabulated accuracy comparisons.
Table 2

Start from the known operation of the Spiking Token Selector (STS) (conclusion 1) and the layer-wise token pruning schedule and insertion points (conclusion 2); treat these as established mechanisms used to produce token-pruned SparseSpikformer models whose runtime and FLOPs are evaluated experimentally.

Describe the evaluation metrics used in the token-pruning experiments: Top-1 accuracy (percentage), Throughput measured in samples per second (samples/s), and Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs) measured in Giga FLOPs (GFLOPs); these are the three metrics reported in the experimental table for different keep ratios $\\rho$.

Report the baseline Spikformer numbers from the experiments (keep ratio $\\rho=1.0$): Top-1 accuracy 94.95%, throughput 950.28 samples/s, and FLOPs 3.74G, as listed in the first row of Table 1 for the CIFAR-10 column.
Table 1

Report the SparseSpikformer numbers for keep ratio $\\rho=0.7$ from Table 1: Top-1 accuracy 95.01%, throughput 1448.71 samples/s, and FLOPs 3.04G for CIFAR-10; these values demonstrate that at $\\rho=0.7$ token pruning yields higher throughput and lower FLOPs, with negligible accuracy change or even a small accuracy gain in this reported case.
Table 1

Generalize the reported improvements across the keep ratios and datasets in Table 1: token pruning reduces FLOPs by approximately 22.49% to 26.47% and increases throughput by approximately 21.98% to 66.96% while preserving Top-1 accuracy within minimal degradation or even small gains for some keep ratios and datasets; state these percentage ranges as reported in the paper's experimental summary.
Table 1

Explain the mechanism that produces these compute/runtime gains: because the STS removes a fraction of image tokens before SSA and MLP at multiple encoder depths (according to the layer-wise schedule), the number of tokens processed by attention and MLP modules is reduced, directly lowering the number of FLOPs and increasing achievable throughput on the evaluated hardware (single NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPU in experiments).
Fig. 3

Start from the established application of IMP to Spikformer (conclusion: IMP workflow with $p=25$, $K=15$ produces highly sparse subnetworks that can be retrained) and treat that result as known; refer to the experimental setup and Table 2 where accuracy of pruned models is reported.
Table 2

Present representative results from the weight-pruning experiments on CIFAR-10 as reported in the accuracy table: for the original Spikformer model, at reported sparsity levels the Top-1 accuracies are (a) 75.90% sparsity -> Top-1 94.78, (b) 86.22% sparsity -> Top-1 94.91, and (c) 93.90% sparsity -> Top-1 94.34; these values are read directly from the tabulated entries in Table 2.
Table 2

Present representative results for SparseSpikformer (the token-pruned variant with keep rate $\\rho=0.7$) from the same table: at 93.90% sparsity the SparseSpikformer achieves Top-1 accuracy 94.97 on CIFAR-10 (Table 2 entry), and intermediate sparsity levels (e.g., 73.26%, 88.74%) show Top-1 accuracies 95.28 and 95.06 respectively as tabulated entries.
Table 2

Synthesize the tabulated observations to state the general empirical claim: across reported sparsity levels (examples include 75.90%, 86.22%, 93.90% and others), the pruned subnetworks preserve Top-1 accuracy with only minor degradation relative to the dense baseline, indicating that IMP identifies highly sparse winning tickets in both Spikformer and SparseSpikformer; note that the table covers multiple datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CIFAR10-DVS, DVS-128) and shows similar minor accuracy changes across them.
Table 2

Conclude that weight pruning via IMP can reduce model parameter count by approximately 90% (i.e., achieve ~90% sparsity) while retaining competitive performance, citing the concrete table entries that show 93.90% sparsity with Top-1 accuracies close to or matching dense-level performance for certain settings (e.g., SparseSpikformer 93.90% -> 94.97 on CIFAR-10).

Define the three LTH-related methods compared: (a) Iterative Magnitude Pruning (IMP) as described earlier (rank-and-prune with rewinding), (b) Early-Bird (EB) ticket detection which attempts to find trainable subnetworks early during training as referenced by the authors, and (c) Random Re-initialization (RR) where pruned subnetworks are reinitialized randomly rather than rewound; include the citation provided for Early-Bird.
[25]

Describe the experimental comparison setup: evaluate the Top-1 accuracy trajectories or final Top-1 accuracies of subnetworks obtained by IMP, EB, and RR on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 across high-sparsity points (examples given include sparsities such as 75.90%, 86.22%, and 92.04%); refer to the figure that pictorially summarizes these accuracy comparisons.
Fig. 4

Report the empirical accuracy differences observed and stated by the authors: IMP consistently outperforms EB and RR for high-sparsity subnetworks, achieving superior Top-1 accuracy margins in the range approximately from $3.52\\%$ up to $9.74\\%$ over EB and RR across the evaluated sparsity points on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 (the paper reports this numeric range as the observed advantage of IMP).

Compare re-initialization strategies explicitly: contrast Random Re-initialization (RR) with Rewinding (the IMP rewinding/reinitialization strategy), and report the authors' experimental observation that rewinding yields winning-ticket accuracies "closer to that of the original network" than RR; record that this is an empirical conclusion based on the same experiments depicted in the accuracy comparison.

Treat as known the STS token-pruning mechanism (conclusion 1), the IMP-based weight-pruning that yields winning tickets at high sparsity (conclusion 3 and conclusion 5), and the measured token-pruning compute/runtime benefits (conclusion 4); these established results form the components combined in the co-design claim.

State the combined storage reduction claim drawn from weight-pruning experiments: IMP identifies subnetworks preserving roughly 10% of original weights (i.e., >~90% parameter pruning) as reported in the experiments and tables, so the co-designed framework can produce models with approximately 10% of original parameters retained.
Table 2

State the combined compute reduction claim drawn from token-pruning experiments: token pruning via STS reduces GFLOPs on the order of approximately 20% — specifically the experiments report FLOPs reductions in the range ~22.49% to ~26.47% for various keep ratios and datasets (these numbers are presented in the Table 1 summary).
Table 1

Provide an example joint outcome for throughput to illustrate practical benefits: the token-pruned case for CIFAR-10 at $\\rho=0.7$ increases throughput from 950.28 samples/s (baseline Spikformer) to 1448.71 samples/s (SparseSpikformer), demonstrating that token pruning alone substantially improves inference throughput; combined with parameter sparsity from IMP, the model becomes both storage- and compute-efficient for hardware deployment.
Table 1

Explain how the two pruning axes complement each other operationally: token pruning (STS) reduces per-inference computational workload by removing uninformative tokens before expensive attention and MLP operations, while weight pruning (IMP) reduces model storage and per-layer computation by removing redundant parameters; together they yield simultaneous reductions in memory footprint and GFLOPs while retaining Top-1 accuracy comparable to the original Spikformer across the evaluated datasets.

Conclude that the combined co-design yields hardware-friendly SparseSpikformer models that (a) can retain approximately 10% of original weights (i.e., achieve >~90% parameter pruning), (b) realize GFLOPs reductions on the order of ~20% (as evidenced by token-pruning figures), and (c) preserve Top-1 accuracy comparable to the dense baseline — supporting the claim that joint token-and-weight pruning is an effective route to make Spikformer hardware-friendly.

open_questions.content: The paper contains no explicitly stated, itemized future-work or open-theory questions; the authors do not enumerate unresolved scientific issues beyond general statements about enabling edge deployment. Therefore, no additional explicit open scientific questions or limitations are provided in the text beyond implicit practical extensions (e.g., hardware-accelerator implementation details, broader dataset scaling) which are not framed by the authors as formal open problems.
